cautions: A check being available is not a reason to play it. Proven case: Ra7+ draws and Rg8+ loses in the same position.
A pinned piece still delivers check — being unable to legally move does not stop a piece attacking the king.

concepts.name: Blockade
concepts.wording: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.

concepts.name: Doubled pawns
concepts.wording: Doubled pawns: two friendly pawns on one file. They cannot defend each other and the rear one is blocked, but the capture that created them usually bought something — a file, the bishop pair, or central control.
cautions: Doubled central pawns frequently increase control and are an asset.
The exchange that doubles them often yields the bishop pair or a usable file, which is the whole point.

concepts.name: Isolated queen's pawn
concepts.wording: An isolated queen's pawn. It cannot be defended by a pawn and the square in front is a permanent hole — but it gives central space, half-open c- and e-files, and outposts beside it. It is an asset while pieces are on and a liability once they come off.
cautions: An isolated queen's pawn is not a weakness on sight. In the standard position measured here the side with the isolani is slightly better (+0.14).
The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.

concepts.name: King safety

cautions: An exposed king is not a losing king. In a proven drawn ending both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter, and centralising them is correct - see the recorded counterexample.
An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.

concepts.name: Passed pawn
concepts.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.

concepts.name: The bishop pair
concepts.wording: The bishop pair: a single bishop is blind to half the board, and two together cover everything. Statistically worth about half a pawn beyond the two bishops separately, and strongest in open positions.
cautions: In a locked position the pair may be worth nothing and a knight may be better.
A bishop shut in by its own pawns does not contribute to the pair.

concepts.name: Bad bishop
concepts.wording: A bad bishop — its own pawns sit on the squares it travels on, so its diagonals are blocked from the inside and the squares they leave uncovered are ones the bishop cannot use either. The cures are a pawn break, a trade, or getting the bishop outside the chain.
cautions: Suba's active bad bishop: outside the pawn chain, a structurally bad bishop is often equal or better than a knight.
A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.

altConcept.name: Blockade
altConcept.wording: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.

concepts.name: Pawn break
concepts.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.
cautions: A break that opens lines for a better-developed opponent helps them.
Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.

concepts.name: Sacrifice

A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.

concepts.name: Passed pawn
concepts.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. concepts.name: Isolated queen's pawn

concepts.name: Exchange sacrifice
concepts.wording: An exchange sacrifice: rook for a minor piece. First check whether it is forced — if mate or material follows by force, calculate it. If not, name the lasting asset it buys.
cautions: In open positions with files available, a rook is worth more than the nominal margin and the sacrifice is correspondingly worse.
Returning the exchange at the right moment is a standard resource for the defender and must be accounted for.

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.wording: A sacrifice. First ask whether the material comes back by force: if it does, calculate it and stop worrying. If it does not, you are judging the compensation instead.
cautions: A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.

concepts.name: The principle of two weaknesses
concepts.wording: A single weak point is holdable because every defender can gather around it. Fix it so it cannot be repaired, improve your own pieces while the opponent has nothing to do, then open a second front on the far wing. The defence cracks in transit between the two, not at either one.

In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.

concepts.name: The bishop pair
concepts.wording: The bishop pair: a single bishop is blind to half the board, and two together cover everything. Statistically worth about half a pawn beyond the two bishops separately, and strongest in open positions.
cautions: In a locked position the pair may be worth nothing and a knight may be better.
A bishop shut in by its own pawns does not contribute to the pair.

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.wording: A sacrifice. First ask whether the material comes back by force: if it does, calculate it and stop worrying. If it does not, you are judging the compensation instead.
cautions: A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.

moves.text: The rook on f8 is pinned to the queen behind it and cannot step aside. It gives up a rook first, which is why it is easy to reject. The next best move, Qf5, only leaves Black clearly worse. A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.

concept.name: Passed pawn
concept.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

moves.text: It takes the rook back. It is the toughest try — nothing else does better.

It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.

concept.name: King safety
concept.wording: King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.
cautions: An exposed king is not a losing king. In a proven drawn ending both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter, and centralising them is correct - see the recorded counterexample.
An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.

moves.text: The king is in check and has to answer it. Everything else is clearly worse for them.

The pawn on a2 is pinned to the rook behind it and cannot step aside. It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. A pin. The pinned piece is stuck and makes a poor defender, so you can pile up on it.

concept.name: Pin
concept.why: The pawn on a2 is pinned to the rook behind it and cannot step aside.
concept.wording: A pin. The pinned piece is stuck and makes a poor defender, so you can pile up on it.
cautions: A pinned piece still delivers check and still guards squares against non-king units.
A relative pin can be broken profitably when moving the front piece creates a bigger threat.

moves.text: The king is in check and has to answer it. It is the toughest try — nothing else does better.

The pawn on f6 is pinned to the queen behind it and cannot step aside. It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. Doubled pawns: two friendly pawns on one file. They cannot defend each other and the rear one is blocked, but the capture that created them usually bought something — a file, the bishop pair, or central control.

concept.name: Doubled pawns
concept.wording: Doubled pawns: two friendly pawns on one file. They cannot defend each other and the rear one is blocked, but the capture that created them usually bought something — a file, the bishop pair, or central control.
cautions: Doubled central pawns frequently increase control and are an asset.
The exchange that doubles them often yields the bishop pair or a usable file, which is the whole point.

moves.text: Forced — it is the only legal move.

The pawn on a2 is pinned to the rook behind it and cannot step aside. It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. Control of the centre: influence over the four central squares, whether by occupying them with pawns or attacking them from a distance with pieces. Occupation gives space; control without commitment avoids giving a target.

concept.name: Control of the centre
concept.wording: Control of the centre: influence over the four central squares, whether by occupying them with pawns or attacking them from a distance with pieces. Occupation gives space; control without commitment avoids giving a target.
cautions: Occupying the centre is not always right — an unsupported pawn centre is a target, which is the hypermodern case.
Ceding the centre is not always right either — against proper support it just loses space.

moves.text: The king is in check and has to answer it. It is the toughest try — nothing else does better.

It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. It wins the pawn. A space advantage: you control more squares behind your pawn front. The value is mobility — their pieces get in each other's way. Avoid exchanges, and find an entry square, because space without a way in wins nothing.

concept.name: Space advantage
concept.wording: A space advantage: you control more squares behind your pawn front. The value is mobility — their pieces get in each other's way. Avoid exchanges, and find an entry square, because space without a way in wins nothing.
cautions: Space with no way in is worth little.
Space bought by overextension is a liability — the hypermodern critique.

why.mistake: White played Qh8. Moving the queen from h7 took the last guard off f5.
why.swing: The position was losing for Black before it and is level after it, with best play.
why.point: Black is a piece down on material, though the engine calls the position only level.
